First 15972 characters: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
abstract: Neural machine translation is a recently proposed approach to machine translation. Unlike the traditional statistical machine translation, the neural machine translation aims at building a single neural network that can be jointly tuned to maximize the translation performance. The models proposed recently for neural machine translation often belong to a family of encoder-decoders and consists of an encoder that encodes a source sentence into a fixed-length vector from which a decoder generates a translation. In this paper, we conjecture that the use of a fixed-length vector is a bottleneck in improving the performance of this basic encoder-decoder architecture, and propose to extend this by allowing a model to automatically (soft-)search for parts of a source sentence that are relevant to predicting a target word, without having to form these parts as a hard segment explicitly. With this new approach, we achieve a translation performance comparable to the existing state-of-the-art phrase-based system on the task of English-to-French translation. Furthermore, qualitative analysis reveals that the (soft-)alignments found by the model agree well with our intuition.
Introduction: Neural machine translation is a newly emerging approach to machine translation, recently proposed by , and . Unlike the traditional phrase-based translation system which consists of many small sub-components that are tuned separately, neural machine translation attempts to build and train a single, large neural network that reads a sentence and outputs a correct translation.Most of the proposed neural machine translation models belong to a family of encoder–decoders , , with an encoder and a decoder for each language, or involve a language-specific encoder applied to each sentence whose outputs are then compared . An encoder neural network reads and encodes a source sentence into a fixed-length vector. A decoder then outputs a translation from the encoded vector. The whole encoder–decoder system, which consists of the encoder and the decoder for a language pair, is jointly trained to maximize the probability of a correct translation given a source sentence.A potential issue with this encoder–decoder approach is that a neural network needs to be able to compress all the necessary information of a source sentence into a fixed-length vector. This may make it difficult for the neural network to cope with long sentences, especially those that are longer than the sentences in the training corpus. showed that indeed the performance of a basic encoder–decoder deteriorates rapidly as the length of an input sentence increases.In order to address this issue, we introduce an extension to the encoder–decoder model which learns to align and translate jointly. Each time the proposed model generates a word in a translation, it (soft-)searches for a set of positions in a source sentence where the most relevant information is concentrated. The model then predicts a target word based on the context vectors associated with these source positions and all the previous generated target words.The most important distinguishing feature of this approach from the basic encoder–decoder is that it does not attempt to encode a whole input sentence into a single fixed-length vector. Instead, it encodes the input sentence into a sequence of vectors and chooses a subset of these vectors adaptively while decoding the translation. This frees a neural translation model from having to squash all the information of a source sentence, regardless of its length, into a fixed-length vector. We show this allows a model to cope better with long sentences.In this paper, we show that the proposed approach of jointly learning to align and translate achieves significantly improved translation performance over the basic encoder–decoder approach. The improvement is more apparent with longer sentences, but can be observed with sentences of any length. On the task of English-to-French translation, the proposed approach achieves, with a single model, a translation performance comparable, or close, to the conventional phrase-based system. Furthermore, qualitative analysis reveals that the proposed model finds a linguistically plausible (soft-)alignment between a source sentence and the corresponding target sentence.
Background: Neural Machine Translation: From a probabilistic perspective, translation is equivalent to finding a target sentence {{formula:46a7661d-ddf5-4475-93b9-64ad04b265b2}} that maximizes the conditional probability of {{formula:ef09ae09-1177-4991-a511-d9c3efd2937c}} given a source sentence {{formula:6acc12f3-9487-47bd-9683-c4931b4bd682}} , i.e., {{formula:f06a821c-3e18-41ea-bd9f-f8604aaa076e}} . In neural machine translation, we fit a parameterized model to maximize the conditional probability of sentence pairs using a parallel training corpus. Once the conditional distribution is learned by a translation model, given a source sentence a corresponding translation can be generated by searching for the sentence that maximizes the conditional probability.Recently, a number of papers have proposed the use of neural networks to directly learn this conditional distribution , , , , . This neural machine translation approach typically consists of two components, the first of which encodes a source sentence {{formula:c0fce891-66f6-477b-bd32-d22032be6f3d}} and the second decodes to a target sentence {{formula:f8a77217-d302-4d37-8983-4f19f06d50be}} . For instance, two recurrent neural networks (RNN) were used by and to encode a variable-length source sentence into a fixed-length vector and to decode the vector into a variable-length target sentence.Despite being a quite new approach, neural machine translation has already shown promising results. reported that the neural machine translation based on RNNs with long short-term memory (LSTM) units achieves close to the state-of-the-art performance of the conventional phrase-based machine translation system on an English-to-French translation task.We mean by the state-of-the-art performance, the performance of the conventional phrase-based system without using any neural network-based component. Adding neural components to existing translation systems, for instance, to score the phrase pairs in the phrase table or to re-rank candidate translations , has allowed to surpass the previous state-of-the-art performance level.
RNN Encoder–Decoder: Here, we describe briefly the underlying framework, called RNN Encoder–Decoder, proposed by and upon which we build a novel architecture that learns to align and translate simultaneously.In the Encoder–Decoder framework, an encoder reads the input sentence, a sequence of vectors {{formula:19ac6149-3618-4077-9cb8-2fbe5da14fd2}} , into a vector {{formula:57964935-585c-4234-906a-390748f1fbc4}} .Although most of the previous works , , used to encode a variable-length input sentence into a fixed-length vector, it is not necessary, and even it may be beneficial to have a variable-length vector, as we will show later. In other words, the decoder defines a probability over the translation {{formula:6a426764-f921-47a9-8888-3f35a9195848}} by decomposing the joint probability into the ordered conditionals: {{formula:406c5319-93c3-409f-a7db-c973187bf07d}}where {{formula:79bce321-0b81-4d39-a20f-00e997717a43}} . With an RNN, each conditional probability is modeled as {{formula:7fde5a07-c934-494a-afe4-d1655f0cfe27}}where {{formula:15022e2e-11ae-4563-9f13-7421e8b52b91}} is a nonlinear, potentially multi-layered, function that outputs the probability of {{formula:2ca6afaf-d8c4-427d-8e10-a5e7824e59bc}} , and {{formula:3fa4c4bb-7f91-4b30-b92b-184163b79566}} is the hidden state of the RNN. It should be noted that other architectures such as a hybrid of an RNN and a de-convolutional neural network can be used .
Learning to Align and Translate: In this section, we propose a novel architecture for neural machine translation. The new architecture consists of a bidirectional RNN as an encoder (Sec. REF ) and a decoder that emulates searching through a source sentence during decoding a translation (Sec. REF ).

Intuitively, this implements a mechanism of attention in the decoder. The decoder decides parts of the source sentence to pay attention to. By letting the decoder have an attention mechanism, we relieve the encoder from the burden of having to encode all information in the source sentence into a fixed-length vector. With this new approach the information can be spread throughout the sequence of annotations, which can be selectively retrieved by the decoder accordingly.
Encoder: Bidirectional RNN for Annotating Sequences: The usual RNN, described in Eq. (REF ), reads an input sequence {{formula:789c9dd8-1b18-4966-b187-0a32e9923d64}} in order starting from the first symbol {{formula:5e3ac36e-1a1a-44e5-8e67-8062a21c2e18}} to the last one {{formula:ac9fa985-b9b7-4c10-a08e-b0717085a406}} . However, in the proposed scheme, we would like the annotation of each word to summarize not only the preceding words, but also the following words. Hence, we propose to use a bidirectional RNN , which has been successfully used recently in speech recognition .A BiRNN consists of forward and backward RNN's. The forward RNN {{formula:198aaa39-12b9-49de-9a76-28051561d329}} reads the input sequence as it is ordered (from {{formula:bff14791-53a3-4940-8bd1-dea7b43af954}} to {{formula:4acf9e2e-71e3-400b-b557-60fc89e5f38b}} ) and calculates a sequence of forward hidden states {{formula:64c7697a-b281-43a6-b8b7-71c920e94be5}} . In this way, the annotation {{formula:96ce0326-6ca4-4e38-a091-932a933f3004}} contains the summaries of both the preceding words and the following words. Experiment Settings: We evaluate the proposed approach on the task of English-to-French translation. We use the bilingual, parallel corpora provided by ACL WMT '14.http://www.statmt.org/wmt14/translation-task.html As a comparison, we also report the performance of an RNN Encoder–Decoder which was proposed recently by . We use the same training procedures and the same dataset for bo   Last 15972 characters: ally, his alignment was restricted to predict the location such that the location increases monotonically.The main difference from our approach is that, in , the modes of the weights of the annotations only move in one direction. In the context of machine translation, this is a severe limitation, as (long-distance) reordering is often needed to generate a grammatically correct translation (for instance, English-to-German).Our approach, on the other hand, requires computing the annotation weight of every word in the source sentence for each word in the translation. This drawback is not severe with the task of translation in which most of input and output sentences are only 15–40 words. However, this may limit the applicability of the proposed scheme to other tasks.
Neural Networks for Machine Translation: Since introduced a neural probabilistic language model which uses a neural network to model the conditional probability of a word given a fixed number of the preceding words, neural networks have widely been used in machine translation. However, the role of neural networks has been largely limited to simply providing a single feature to an existing statistical machine translation system or to re-rank a list of candidate translations provided by an existing system.For instance, proposed using a feedforward neural network to compute the score of a pair of source and target phrases and to use the score as an additional feature in the phrase-based statistical machine translation system. More recently, and reported the successful use of the neural networks as a sub-component of the existing translation system. Traditionally, a neural network trained as a target-side language model has been used to rescore or rerank a list of candidate translations .Although the above approaches were shown to improve the translation performance over the state-of-the-art machine translation systems, we are more interested in a more ambitious objective of designing a completely new translation system based on neural networks. The neural machine translation approach we consider in this paper is therefore a radical departure from these earlier works. Rather than using a neural network as a part of the existing system, our model works on its own and generates a translation from a source sentence directly.
Conclusion: The conventional approach to neural machine translation, called an encoder–decoder approach, encodes a whole input sentence into a fixed-length vector from which a translation will be decoded. We conjectured that the use of a fixed-length context vector is problematic for translating long sentences, based on a recent empirical study reported by and .In this paper, we proposed a novel architecture that addresses this issue. We extended the basic encoder–decoder by letting a model (soft-)search for a set of input words, or their annotations computed by an encoder, when generating each target word. This frees the model from having to encode a whole source sentence into a fixed-length vector, and also lets the model focus only on information relevant to the generation of the next target word. This has a major positive impact on the ability of the neural machine translation system to yield good results on longer sentences. Unlike with the traditional machine translation systems, all of the pieces of the translation system, including the alignment mechanism, are jointly trained towards a better log-probability of producing correct translations.We tested the proposed model, called RNNsearch, on the task of English-to-French translation. The experiment revealed that the proposed RNNsearch outperforms the conventional encoder–decoder model (RNNencdec) significantly, regardless of the sentence length and that it is much more robust to the length of a source sentence. From the qualitative analysis where we investigated the (soft-)alignment generated by the RNNsearch, we were able to conclude that the model can correctly align each target word with the relevant words, or their annotations, in the source sentence as it generated a correct translation.Perhaps more importantly, the proposed approach achieved a translation performance comparable to the existing phrase-based statistical machine translation. It is a striking result, considering that the proposed architecture, or the whole family of neural machine translation, has only been proposed as recently as this year. We believe the architecture proposed here is a promising step toward better machine translation and a better understanding of natural languages in general.One of challenges left for the future is to better handle unknown, or rare words. This will be required for the model to be more widely used and to match the performance of current state-of-the-art machine translation systems in all contexts.

(REF )) as a multi-layered function . We use a single hidden layer of maxout units and normalize the output probabilities (one for each word) with a softmax function (see Eq. (REF )).
Alignment Model: The alignment model should be designed considering that the model needs to be evaluated {{formula:29dc6047-ba6f-439e-8097-3150f047ecda}} times for each sentence pair of lengths {{formula:dd44d206-9367-4bfc-83bd-530a95222a74}} and {{formula:91f510d5-09ff-4468-8f0e-1fb419307de2}} . In order to reduce computation, we use a single-layer multilayer perceptron such that {{formula:e6a18cc5-89e1-418b-8afe-7d4ba13968d0}}where {{formula:976d6f1b-d69d-49af-9583-c3971f4555e5}} and {{formula:8e11b6e0-3236-4b7e-8b1d-4305681c34d5}} are the weight matrices. Since {{formula:b6809909-d53e-43f2-88d0-e7db78fd37d4}} does not depend on {{formula:546cc9e1-b7c0-4e6f-b1fe-b5404f140841}} , we can pre-compute it in advance to minimize the computational cost.
Encoder: In this section, we describe in detail the architecture of the proposed model (RNNsearch) used in the experiments (see Sec. –). From here on, we omit all bias terms in order to increase readability.The model takes a source sentence of 1-of-K coded word vectors as input {{formula:d2f71340-afd6-4c8f-8d72-cb3f4c3b427c}}and outputs a translated sentence of 1-of-K coded word vectors {{formula:c4089bd6-b88a-4061-b7b8-911cf17224df}}where {{formula:9091e343-0fa1-4e7d-964a-45dce3b4282b}} and {{formula:1e18806a-5866-4d43-b998-c64dfc15e516}} are the vocabulary sizes of source and target languages, respectively. {{formula:469834e0-4bfc-459d-8f93-9c61b253960d}} and {{formula:4961c75b-866a-40b7-aeb4-ed83a79d3d7d}} respectively denote the lengths of source and target sentences.First, the forward states of the bidirectional recurrent neural network (BiRNN) are computed: {{formula:3e382312-b7c4-4c41-a46a-bd2ba873ceaf}}where {{formula:d975205e-d4bc-4f0b-b73b-1bf4171db2f1}}{{formula:772fe372-88e1-4c41-8c06-5647ac2640b7}} is the word embedding matrix. {{formula:b034e5b5-6ae7-4499-a214-3cec4e7ade31}} , {{formula:d8db41bc-f6ea-4abe-a4f0-7c506fdc46ce}} are weight matrices. {{formula:57c0fe38-6ef2-4393-8326-f4249b826b62}} and {{formula:c93a11db-d089-42f0-97ff-d87fcc39e1ed}} are the word embedding dimensionality and the number of hidden units, respectively. {{formula:9a89be74-7f94-4120-8c1e-2c65ce76bca3}} is as usual a logistic sigmoid function.The backward states {{formula:7b0a1946-3844-4e30-9a69-a54956b29977}} are computed similarly. We share the word embedding matrix {{formula:4493b11c-743e-4743-b4be-71142a7f88ea}} between the forward and backward RNNs, unlike the weight matrices.We concatenate the forward and backward states to to obtain the annotations {{formula:92dfb53e-927e-4bc0-90ba-5c49727e058f}} , where {{formula:e8e591bb-8704-48bd-ba03-8c50a42aa76a}}
Decoder: The hidden state {{formula:eb79c4f5-e840-4646-b4e2-5b9f2d802a92}} of the decoder given the annotations from the encoder is computed by {{formula:126e75cf-c9d9-462e-9d7e-93b22a210a94}}where {{formula:685cb339-3ef0-4146-8c29-ef7f4c2f5ab2}}{{formula:91529dcb-be7b-439d-b1fe-8e1dbbcc8416}} is the word embedding matrix for the target language. {{formula:9cf00863-d8d3-4904-acd1-6d9dc610f853}} , {{formula:e75b27bb-2ef1-4c4a-9b47-aab719a2e624}} , and {{formula:303f6331-c823-4cd8-b539-862c9c599303}} are weights. Again, {{formula:10b073b8-e6c1-4265-9257-17cfc0b225fa}} and {{formula:925581ce-0be6-42a5-ac33-1cea3dd619b7}} are the word embedding dimensionality and the number of hidden units, respectively. The initial hidden state {{formula:32338b27-d2f0-45a1-b623-07dd8695a68c}} is computed by {{formula:e25b4380-2148-4e37-aaa1-4ad8b275522b}} where {{formula:97490fab-c284-45c8-bd31-0300912c2d58}} .The context vector {{formula:bd3f6d58-0156-4d27-84b7-f765af860bcf}} are recomputed at each step by the alignment model: {{formula:52c038ca-9255-47a3-82ae-f63d76abcf10}}where {{formula:e45bcb15-8c59-4d76-b796-9d2da7937760}}and {{formula:9cdeec29-fe63-456c-9f5b-6fbe9e5327a9}} is the {{formula:754b1234-bd63-4325-816a-848f2e6c4f99}} -th annotation in the source sentence (see Eq. (REF )). {{formula:dd8377e1-6d68-403d-8e3c-3cb170975b87}} and {{formula:35e856c1-107d-4d3f-99de-4b464c197c7e}} are weight matrices. Note that the model becomes RNN Encoder–Decoder , if we fix {{formula:d227ce8e-a1d8-4f96-a7cd-b154cf7bbfa1}} to {{formula:c934abec-be76-4b6f-9a2b-a46d0175714d}} .With the decoder state {{formula:b404d2d5-422b-455f-a417-cc9e94d4fee7}} , the context {{formula:94b19875-2e26-452b-bbb8-2b29bb6303ae}} and the last generated word {{formula:f1b17063-0517-4cce-b4cf-1353b209f1bb}} , we define the probability of a target word {{formula:aa1a36c0-f0a9-49ce-9892-f142014a8873}} as {{formula:a184f03a-fc96-4a0b-80bd-ed6cf611320f}}where {{formula:c0157f1c-297a-428b-a2ee-180f6fc60aae}}and {{formula:e2913cb7-787b-4cc9-83df-d742361cea4c}} is the {{formula:c1a37590-23b6-455a-970a-f7333316e569}} -th element of a vector {{formula:85a1cb0a-341d-4940-bb1d-6edafa8b18f6}} which is computed by {{formula:17ce748c-02a9-4b0d-910a-754048c5ba93}}{{formula:fe8121d1-3cbe-43f3-b672-fd1249753eb6}} , {{formula:c022d1c7-a1ad-49a8-b853-7e3d6568cfe4}} , {{formula:2805e899-1e91-4e29-819d-962c9e949323}} and {{formula:7791b1d4-031a-4bd2-8809-6137a3b97b2c}} are weight matrices. This can be understood as having a deep output with a single maxout hidden layer .
Model Size: For all the models used in this paper, the size of a hidden layer {{formula:b9887aec-4da7-4965-8a9c-9c926cb4ee3e}} is 1000, the word embedding dimensionality {{formula:5063d3f0-7cba-4fd6-9632-8f1be1fb47e8}} is 620 and the size of the maxout hidden layer in the deep output {{formula:ed494cd0-066b-48a3-ab81-1945a3c9308c}} is 500. The number of hidden units in the alignment model {{formula:7061280e-f598-4771-aeed-bfd966c0e9d1}} is 1000. {{table:5be8469c-3b0d-448d-b9c1-5cb92215b14e}}
Parameter Initialization: We initialized the recurrent weight matrices {{formula:33864f70-b07d-417e-8978-d72ab3b636da}} and {{formula:1525beb1-57bb-4128-92a9-016ac19989ba}} as random orthogonal matrices. For {{formula:77b43dca-0519-4419-9d28-be19b4dfaa0f}} and {{formula:676d9629-cd38-47d5-a0b7-390636104ea6}} , we initialized them by sampling each element from the Gaussian distribution of mean 0 and variance {{formula:e5fd9216-06e2-4bc6-a19b-cfecf4c74843}} . All the elements of {{formula:c6f92d9c-fd7b-4f04-b58a-5e30722d417b}} and all the bias vectors were initialized to zero. Any other weight matrix was initialized by sampling from the Gaussian distribution of mean 0 and variance {{formula:981775bb-8770-46ab-a7c6-f350e412663a}} .
Training: We used the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm. Adadelta was used to automatically adapt the learning rate of each parameter ({{formula:542605d0-860c-4f91-85f8-cfb0deda5de1}} and {{formula:9faa0cc5-d6f6-4076-827b-a73f25200d4e}} ). We explicitly normalized the {{formula:af7a54d9-d7b4-48f6-8acb-441d0b45b611}} -norm of the gradient of the cost function each time to be at most a predefined threshold of 1, when the norm was larger than the threshold . Each SGD update direction was computed with a minibatch of 80 sentences.At each update our implementation requires time proportional to the length of the longest sentence in a minibatch. Hence, to minimize the waste of computation, before every 20-th update, we retrieved 1600 sentence pairs, sorted them according to the lengths and split them into 20 minibatches. The training data was shuffled once before training and was traversed sequentially in this manner.In Tables REF we present the statistics related to training all the models used in the experiments.

First 15704 characters: Show, Attend and Tell: Neural Image Caption Generation with Visual Attention
abstract: Inspired by recent work in machine translation and object detection, we introduce an attention based model that automatically learns to describe the content of images. We describe how we can train this model in a deterministic manner using standard backpropagation techniques and stochastically by maximizing a variational lower bound. We also show through visualization how the model is able to automatically learn to fix its gaze on salient objects while generating the corresponding words in the output sequence. We validate the use of attention with state-of-the-art performance on three benchmark datasets: Flickr8k, Flickr30k and MS COCO.
Introduction: Automatically generating captions of an image is a task very close to the heart of scene understanding — one of the primary goals of computer vision. Not only must caption generation models be powerful enough to solve the computer vision challenges of determining which objects are in an image, but they must also be capable of capturing and expressing their relationships in a natural language. For this reason, caption generation has long been viewed as a difficult problem. It is a very important challenge for machine learning algorithms, as it amounts to mimicking the remarkable human ability to compress huge amounts of salient visual infomation into descriptive language.Despite the challenging nature of this task, there has been a recent surge of research interest in attacking the image caption generation problem. Aided by advances in training neural networks and large classification datasets , recent work has significantly improved the quality of caption generation using a combination of convolutional neural networks (convnets) to obtain vectorial representation of images and recurrent neural networks to decode those representations into natural language sentences (see Sec. ). {{figure:23b2632e-a5a9-4bc7-8b71-90740e3ec2f0}}{{figure:8fdd5764-cbe2-4fc8-9a50-5c287077cadd}}{{figure:6f38db8a-13ae-493e-b0f9-b2f0d4f96d8f}}One of the most curious facets of the human visual system is the presence of attention , . Rather than compress an entire image into a static representation, attention allows for salient features to dynamically come to the forefront as needed. This is especially important when there is a lot of clutter in an image. Using representations (such as those from the top layer of a convnet) that distill information in image down to the most salient objects is one effective solution that has been widely adopted in previous work. Unfortunately, this has one potential drawback of losing information which could be useful for richer, more descriptive captions. Using more low-level representation can help preserve this information. However working with these features necessitates a powerful mechanism to steer the model to information important to the task at hand.In this paper, we describe approaches to caption generation that attempt to incorporate a form of attention with two variants: a “hard” attention mechanism and a “soft” attention mechanism. We also show how one advantage of including attention is the ability to visualize what the model “sees”. Encouraged by recent advances in caption generation and inspired by recent success in employing attention in machine translation and object recognition , , we investigate models that can attend to salient part of an image while generating its caption.The contributions of this paper are the following:We introduce two attention-based image caption generators under a common framework (Sec. REF ): 1) a “soft” deterministic attention mechanism trainable by standard back-propagation methods and 2) a “hard” stochastic attention mechanism trainable by maximizing an approximate variational lower bound or equivalently by REINFORCE . We show how we can gain insight and interpret the results of this framework by visualizing “where” and “what” the attention focused on. (see Sec. REF ) Finally, we quantitatively validate the usefulness of attention in caption generation with state of the art performance (Sec. REF ) on three benchmark datasets: Flickr8k , Flickr30k and the MS COCO dataset .
Related Work: In this section we provide relevant background on previous work on image caption generation and attention. Recently, several methods have been proposed for generating image descriptions. Many of these methods are based on recurrent neural networks and inspired by the successful use of sequence to sequence training with neural networks for machine translation , , . One major reason image caption generation is well suited to the encoder-decoder framework of machine translation is because it is analogous to “translating” an image to a sentence.The first approach to use neural networks for caption generation was , who proposed a multimodal log-bilinear model that was biased by features from the image. This work was later followed by whose method was designed to explicitly allow a natural way of doing both ranking and generation. took a similar approach to generation but replaced a feed-forward neural language model with a recurrent one. Both and use LSTM RNNs for their models. Unlike and whose models see the image at each time step of the output word sequence, only show the image to the RNN at the beginning. Along with images, also apply LSTMs to videos, allowing their model to generate video descriptions.All of these works represent images as a single feature vector from the top layer of a pre-trained convolutional network. instead proposed to learn a joint embedding space for ranking and generation whose model learns to score sentence and image similarity as a function of R-CNN object detections with outputs of a bidirectional RNN. proposed a three-step pipeline for generation by incorporating object detections. Their model first learn detectors for several visual concepts based on a multi-instance learning framework. A language model trained on captions was then applied to the detector outputs, followed by rescoring from a joint image-text embedding space. Unlike these models, our proposed attention framework does not explicitly use object detectors but instead learns latent alignments from scratch. This allows our model to go beyond “objectness” and learn to attend to abstract concepts.Prior to the use of neural networks for generating captions, two main approaches were dominant. The first involved generating caption templates which were filled in based on the results of object detections and attribute discovery ( , , , , ). The second approach was based on first retrieving similar captioned images from a large database then modifying these retrieved captions to fit the query , . These approaches typically involved an intermediate “generalization” step to remove the specifics of a caption that are only relevant to the retrieved image, such as the name of a city. Both of these approaches have since fallen out of favour to the now dominant neural network methods.There has been a long line of previous work incorporating attention into neural networks for vision related tasks. Some that share the same spirit as our work include , , . In particular however, our work directly extends the work of , , .
Model Details: In this section, we describe the two variants of our attention-based model by first describing their common framework. The main difference is the definition of the {{formula:da4c0919-8729-4fff-b7e7-2963159b99d4}} function which we describe in detail in Section . We denote vectors with bolded font and matrices with capital letters. In our description below, we suppress bias terms for readability.
Encoder: Convolutional Features: Our model takes a single raw image and generates a caption {{formula:48843f49-dc63-4adc-a3d7-8271c0e495e0}} encoded as a sequence of 1-of-{{formula:c96d0dc9-47f5-498d-8665-f4e0b250c39a}} encoded words. {{formula:8321572b-c96e-4930-b11b-acabea8553c1}}where {{formula:ae77934d-e57e-4eb3-8ba4-9be35abd303a}} is the size of the vocabulary and {{formula:d11c48c0-761f-4218-a477-f1b270b087b9}} is the length of the caption.We use a convolutional neural network in order to extract a set of feature vectors which we refer to as annotation vectors. The extractor produces {{formula:77d7a5d7-ad66-4222-88e2-013e9b7810b8}} vectors, each of which is a D-dimensional representation corresponding to a part of the image. {{formula:76c96bb5-c91a-42cf-bf94-6a661952447a}}In order to obtain a correspondence between the feature vectors and portions of the 2-D image, we extract features from a lower convolutional layer unlike previous work which instead used a fully connected layer. This allows the decoder to selectively focus on certain parts of an image by selecting a subset of all the feature vectors. {{figure:75f9bf42-8b82-4889-9f45-249d3427b4bd}}
Decoder: Long Short-Term Memory Network: We use a long short-term memory (LSTM) network that produces a caption by generating one word at every time step conditioned on a context vector, the previous hidden state and the previously generated words. Our implementation of LSTM closely follows the one used in (see Fig. REF ). Using {{formula:628da3fc-69c3-4a4f-851b-b57a18f1ca2a}} to denote a simple affine transformation with parameters that are learned, {{formula:c1acd303-4e29-4c0e-9e3d-7cec2aaa9f0e}}Here, {{formula:b041f3d3-e273-4b9f-b714-40288d196043}} , {{formula:906c154b-6f51-4f54-9807-c40aea6cbad3}} , {{formula:c90458e8-09dd-4e3d-9af0-b44746c6a875}} , {{formula:e83455e8-a81a-4283-899c-76df04f5bc31}} , {{formula:5a3b41e3-dc2c-4f96-8635-7f4e0aef45f8}} are the input, forget, memory, output and hidden state of the LSTM, respectively. The vector {{formula:54c8c661-85a6-4e84-a489-931a81a0995f}} is the context vector, capturing the visual information associated with a particular input location, as explained below. {{formula:df148e65-9e61-4a15-9901-73917e5fa744}} is an embedding matrix. Let {{formula:d887e53e-c894-4efa-bc02-f2fefc0ffe9c}} and {{formula:f31ddbe4-5826-43a1-8968-3babdd18aa95}} denote the embedding and LSTM dimensionality respectively and {{formula:e160e0b6-bfbb-4b3f-8f51-86c9c71e5787}} and {{formula:c546a7b5-aabb-4279-9ce8-425080c43858}} be the logistic sigmoid activation and element-wise multiplication respectively.In simple terms, the context vector {{formula:caf03712-616f-4c15-b4bc-a5fe0e2a48e3}} (equations (REF )–()) is a dynamic representation of the relevant part of the image input at time {{formula:aaafece9-c906-4e4e-86b3-3572d01940c7}} . We define a mechanism {{formula:b3b732c1-c72b-4f39-9634-23a55a88c3d7}} that computes {{formula:233b0910-d367-4948-b67f-d07fa1ba9d8a}} from the annotation vectors {{formula:c3f3309d-e4b6-4784-a507-eb6a6fe44ff3}} corresponding to the features extracted at different image locations. For each location {{formula:df20cb76-230d-4f5e-ba97-8edfe973786b}} , the mechanism generates a positive weight {{formula:91b0084c-8219-42ba-bd5f-5a772ccb302c}} which can be interpreted either as the probability that location {{formula:9515804e-3711-4adb-b4e6-59cbf2c1f548}} is the right place to focus for producing the next word (the “hard” but stochastic attention mechanism), or as the relative importance to give to location {{formula:d6d7bbcc-b4c6-4534-9557-01dc7f877f7a}} in blending the {{formula:0c9cf62b-7862-451c-a419-d45ebdb5d187}} 's together. The weight {{formula:4d6adeb1-e764-4139-9a96-69cfea87e9e3}} of each annotation vector {{formula:eb91e951-60df-4c9a-8df3-1eaffa76547a}} is computed by an attention model {{formula:e3a19409-0ba6-42f5-a813-c78c51a06828}} for which we use a multilayer perceptron conditioned on the previous hidden state {{formula:5f1b4b50-d52e-4182-a17e-c1b43f18c0b2}} . The soft version of this attention mechanism was introduced by . For emphasis, we note that the hidden state varies as the output RNN advances in its output sequence: “where” the network looks next depends on the sequence of words that has already been generated. {{formula:4a815c9f-8ff6-4924-887d-a6e3d968924e}}Once the weights (which sum to one) are computed, the context vector {{formula:4cfcf543-b571-4c97-8f8e-4fed510241a7}} is computed by {{formula:08545920-50e5-421f-b98e-9e3fbf3da315}}where {{formula:b94239a4-403e-4d03-bd30-d9c681403af3}} is a function that returns a single vector given the set of annotation vectors and their corresponding weights. The details of {{formula:2045e9df-7b13-440f-85d0-1a01cae5bef5}} function are discussed in Sec. .The initial memory state and hidden state of the LSTM are predicted by an average of the annotation vectors fed through two separate MLPs ({{formula:d78c81a4-b49b-4ed0-b508-f9afe54cc9f9}} and {{formula:661e3921-22f7-41ce-85c5-7e7297d9428f}} ): {{formula:b5ac08d0-5e3a-4520-a38b-92f514b8d981}}In this work, we use a deep output layer to compute the output word probability given the LSTM state, the context vector and the previous word: {{formula:db69bae1-7673-4dda-b360-9a04265167e8}}Where {{formula:6e57f424-3d05-4250-862c-258d7fdabb61}} , {{formula:f82606cf-f3a3-4455-9ee3-9fb44ff750a3}} , {{formula:feee6fc1-fbdd-47d9-97a8-e76643bf53de}} , and {{formula:7bcca4c3-b917-4c62-8713-ac0708c10221}} are learned parameters initialized randomly.
Learning Stochastic “Hard” vs Deterministic “Soft” Attention: In this section we discuss two alternative mechanisms for the attention model {{formula:6b71a6ce-cfc5-43ae-8415-cf7f2bbe6f44}} : stochastic attention and deterministic attention. {{figure:1d73b6e2-e13e-46d2-b056-7e3b1d4ada29}}
Stochastic “Hard” Attention: We represent the location variable {{formula:1c7c06c5-87f8-4f6c-adb6-ce5e0a94bc89}} as where the model decides to focus attention when generating the {{formula:e98480c5-9517-48ee-9680-6fc3e41636a9}} word. {{formula:dabaad08-dc90-4fd2-9508-bc5fce9813df}} is an indicator one-hot variable which is set to 1 if the {{formula:fc035d4e-66ff-4359-996f-d1313e019719}} -th location (out of {{formula:6ce8a01a-a476-45f8-9d83-bb996e7e32ad}} ) is the one used to extract visual features. By treating the attention locations as intermediate latent variables, we can assign a multinoulli distribution parametrized by {{formula:93ab82c1-b1ab-4d12-8788-58076cd7e2cb}} , and view {{formula:08a6ec43-ff96-466f-8a40-2319c590ecdb}} as a random variable: {{formula:9d4b3e11-28d0-4b85-8b75-2fe02414202d}}We define a new objective function {{formula:4da3acd3-645b-4070-a9cd-6704b31dbb0e}} that is a variational lower bound on the marginal log-likelihood {{formula:67bc50c3-fe3c-4f4b-9b08-2a8c0f7ab1bd}} of observing the sequence of words {{formula:45e38619-03cc-4f2a-93a9-a679bddee740}} given image features {{formula:296b6dc7-ae2b-43f8-a42d-6484c2e6d16b}} . The learning algorithm for the parameters {{formula:08f9367b-bec9-4a35-8b22-5b3838b5c20f}} of the models can be derived by directly optimizing {{formula:a11b641f-3a9f-40a2-8905-469da733bf65}} : {{formula:cda9fb58-d558-4c71-ac77-e4d52039a6a2}} {{formula:a2866e32-c950-4e2b-8467-c957ff82fb9a}}Equation REF suggests a Monte Carlo based sampling approximation of the gradient with respect to the model parameters. This can be done by sampling the location {{formula:de8358b4-dbbf-419b-ae30-87288e034576}} from a multinouilli distribution defined by Equation REF . {{formula:eb444e20-c260-46e5-ba1d-828f1247417f}} {{formula:7331d158-23c5-482a-92b6-de88b2d5df48}}A moving average baseline is used to reduce the variance in the Monte Carlo estimator of the gradient, following . Training Procedure: Both variants of our attention model were trained with stochastic gradient descent using adaptive learning rate algorithms. For the Flickr8k dataset, we found that RMSProp worked best, while for Flickr30k/MS COCO dataset we used the recently proposed Adam algorithm .To create the annotations {{formula:224ada62-c175-4776-9794-72d96ce7342d}} used by our decoder, we used the Oxford VGGnet pre-trained on ImageNet without finetuning. In principle however, any encoding function could be used. In addition, with enough data, we could also train the encoder from scratch (or fine-tune) with the rest of the model. In our experiments we use the 14{{formula:65c9ace1-98c0-48af-b1aa-c0530fc66554}} 14{{formula:8606f6e4-7ce5-454f-9baf-c1eaacafa30d}} 512 feature map of the fourth convolutional layer before max pooling. This means our decoder operates on the flattened 196 {{formula:edf4e857-194c-43f2-a504-48e8bb9ec065}} 512 (i.e {{formula:3bce8fb2-6adf-4b42-a0f1-358e7ec6476a}} ) encoding.As our implementation requires time proportional to the length of the longest sentence per update, we found training on a random group of captions to be computationally wasteful. To mitigate this problem, in preprocessing we build a dictionary mapping the length of a sentence to the corresponding subset of captions. Then, during training we randomly sample a length and retrieve a mini-batch of size 64 of that length. We found that this greatly improved convergence speed with no noticeable diminishment in performance. On our largest dataset (MS COCO), our soft attention model took less than 3 days to train on an NVIDIA Titan Black GPU.In addition to dropout , the only other regularization strategy we used was early stopping on BLEU score. We observed a breakdown in correlation between the validation set log-likelihood and BLEU in the later stages of training during our experiments. Since BLEU is the most commonly reported metric, we used BLEU on our validation set for model selection.In our experiments with soft attention, we also used Whetlabhttps://www.whetlab.com/ , in our Flickr8k experiments. Some of the intuitions we gained from hyperparameter regions it explored were especially important in our Flickr30k and COCO experiments.We make our code for these models based in Theano publicly available upon publication to encourage future research in this area.
Experiments: We describe our experimental methodology and quantitative results which validate the effectiveness of our model for caption generation.
Data: We report results on the popular Flickr8k and Flickr30k dataset which has 8,000 and 30,000 images respectively as well as the more challenging Microsoft COCO dataset which has 82,783 images. The Flickr8k/Flickr30k dataset both come with 5 reference sentences per image, but for the MS COCO dataset, some of the images have references in excess of 5 which for consistency across our datasets we discard. We applied only basic tokenization to MS COCO so that it is consistent with the tokenization present in Flickr8k and Flickr30k. For all our experiments, we used a fixed vocabulary size of 10,000.Results for our attention-based architecture are reported in Table REF . We report results with the frequently used BLEU metricWe verified that our BLEU evaluation code matches the authors of , and . For fairness, we only compare against results for which we have verified that our BLEU evaluation code is the same. With the upcoming release of the COCO evaluation server, we will include comparison results with all other recent image captioning models. which is the standard in the caption generation literature. We report BLEU from 1 to 4 without a brevity penalty. There has been, however, criticism of BLEU, so in addition we report another common metric METEOR , and compare whenever possible.
Evaluation Procedures: A few challenges exist for comparison, which we explain here. The first is a difference in choice of convolutional feature extractor. For identical decoder architectures, using more recent architectures such as GoogLeNet or Oxford VGG , can give a boost in performance over using the AlexNet . In our evaluation, we compare directly only with results which use the comparable GoogLeNet/Oxford VGG features, but for METEOR comparison we note some results that use AlexNet.The second challenge is a single model versus ensemble comparison. While other methods have reported performance boosts by using ensembling, in our results we report a single model performance.Finally, there is challenge due to differences between dataset splits. In our reported results, we use the pre-defined splits of Flickr8k. However, one challenge for the Flickr30k and COCO datasets is the lack of standardized splits. As a result, we report with the publicly available splitshttp://cs.stanford.edu/people/karpathy/deepimagesent/ used in previous work . In our experience, differences in splits do not make a substantial difference in overall performance, but we note the differences where they exist.
Quantitative Analysis: In Table REF , we provide a summary of the experiment validating the quantitative effectiveness of attention. We obtain state of the art performance on the Flickr8k, Flickr30k and MS COCO. In addition, we note that in our experiments we are able to significantly improve the state of the art performance METEOR on MS COCO that we speculate is connected to some of the regularization techniques we used REF and our lower level representation. Finally, we also note that we are able to obtain this performance using a single model without an ensemble.
Qualitative Analysis: Learning to attend: By visualizing the attention component learned by the model, we are able to add an extra layer of interpretability to the output of the model (see Fig. 1). Other systems that have done this rely on object detection systems to produce candidate alignment targets . Our approach is much more flexible, since the model can attend to “non object” salient regions.The 19-layer OxfordNet uses stacks of 3x3 filters meaning the only time the feature maps decrease in size are due to the max pooling layers. The input image is resized so that the shortest side is 256 dimensional with preserved aspect ratio. The input to the convolutional network is the center cropped 224x224 image. Consequently, with 4 max pooling layers we get an output dimension of the top convolutional layer of 14x14. Thus in order to visualize the attention weights for the soft model, we simply upsample the weights by a factor of {{formula:cce0d36e-8009-4899-bb40-1ae5683c5e9d}} = 16 and apply a Gaussian filter. We note that the receptive fields of each of the 14x14 units are highly overlapping.As we can see in Figure 2 and 3, the model learns alignments that correspond very strongly with human intuition. Especially in the examples of mistakes, we see that it is possible to exploit such visualizations to get an intuition as to why those mistakes were made. We provide a more extensive list of visualizations in Appendix for the reader.
Conclusion: We propose an attention based approach that gives state of the art performance on three benchmark datasets using the BLEU and METEOR metric. We also show how the learned attention can be exploited to give more interpretability into the models generation process, and demonstrate that the learned alignments correspond very well to human intuition. We hope that the results of this paper will encourage future work in using visual attention. We also expect that the modularity of the encoder-decoder approach combined with attention to have useful applications in other domains.

claims.claim: The image encoder must provide annotation vectors from a lower convolutional feature map rather than a fully connected layer because this preserves spatial correspondence needed for the attention mechanism.

This structural requirement mirrors the properties of annotations in sequence‑to‑sequence attention models for text, where each annotation corresponds to a specific position in the source sequence, enabling the decoder to attend to localized parts of the input.

multiHopValidity.explanation: The question asks two distinct but related sub‑questions: (1) why an image encoder must output annotation vectors from a lower convolutional layer, and (2) how this mirrors the role of annotations in text‑based sequence‑to‑sequence attention models. The first sub‑question is answered by the image‑captioning paper (Show, Attend and Tell), which discusses spatial correspondence and the inadequacy of a fully connected layer. The second sub‑question is answered by the neural‑machine‑translation paper (Bahdanau et al.), which defines annotations as position‑specific vectors that enable localized attention. Neither paper alone can answer the whole question, and the question does not leak the answer. Therefore, both papers are strictly required, making the multi‑hop validity of the question GOOD.

thinking.step1Claim: In sequence‑to‑sequence attention models the encoder produces a sequence of annotation vectors, where each annotation is tied to a specific position (or local region) of the input sequence. The decoder then forms a context vector as a weighted sum of these annotations, which requires that each annotation be localized so the alignment model can score the relevance of each distinct input part independently.

step1NotTrivial.explanation: The claim is a conceptual mechanism about how attention works (localised annotations enabling weighted summation), not merely the name of a method, dataset or metric.

step1LeakedByQuestion.explanation: The question asks why the image encoder must provide lower‑layer annotation vectors and how this mirrors the properties of text annotations, but it does not state the localisation requirement itself. The answer must derive that property from the first paper.

thinking.step2Claim: In the image‑captioning model the encoder extracts annotation vectors from a lower convolutional feature map (e.g., the 14×14 grid of the fourth conv layer) instead of a fully‑connected layer, because this preserves a spatial grid where each vector corresponds to a specific image region, enabling the attention decoder to attend to individual regions.

strictDependency.explanation: Understanding why spatially localised vectors are needed hinges on the principle from step 1 that attention operates over a set of localized annotations. Without that principle, one could describe the architectural choice but not justify it as a necessary consequence of the attention mechanism.

entityLinking.explanation: Step 1 is not just an entity name; it is a mechanism. Step 2 is not merely tracking that entity across papers; it applies the mechanism to explain a design decision.

dependencyStrength.explanation: The question requires two distinct reasoning steps. Step 1 extracts a non‑trivial mechanism from the neural‑machine‑translation paper: attention needs a sequence of localized annotation vectors. Step 2 extracts an observation from the image‑captioning paper: the encoder must use lower‑layer convolutional features to obtain such localized vectors. Answering step 2 correctly depends on applying the principle from step 1; without it the justification for the architectural choice would be incomplete. The steps are not just entity linking, and the question does not leak the step 1 proposition. Therefore the dependency is strong and the multihop question satisfies the GOOD criterion.

thinking.mainQuestion: Explain why, in attention‑based image captioning, the encoder must supply annotation vectors taken from a lower convolutional feature map instead of a fully‑connected layer, and relate this design choice to the nature of annotation vectors in sequence‑to‑sequence attention models for text.

subquestions.question: Why must the image encoder provide annotation vectors from a lower convolutional feature map rather than a fully connected layer?
How does this structural requirement reflect the properties of annotations in sequence‑to‑sequence attention models for text?

concatenationOrComparison.explanation: The final answer is not a simple concatenation of two independent facts; it must explain how the need for spatially localized annotation vectors in images follows from the same principle that text annotations are position‑specific vectors used by the attention mechanism.

onePartConstrainsOther.explanation: Understanding why lower‑level convolutional features are required depends on the property that annotations must correspond to distinct input positions, a concept described in the text‑based attention model. Thus the answer to the first sub‑question is constrained by the explanation of the second.

artificialIntegration.explanation: The question is not artificially integrated; the integration is essential because the justification for the image‑side design directly invokes the definition of annotations from the text‑side model.

necessaryExplanatoryBridge.explanation: A genuine explanatory bridge is needed: one must synthesize the idea that attention operates over a set of localized annotation vectors (from the text model) and therefore the image encoder must produce analogous localized vectors (from a convolutional map).

nonDecomposability.explanation: The question requires multi‑hop reasoning. The first part (image encoder design) is answered by the Show, Attend and Tell paper, which states that using a lower convolutional layer preserves spatial correspondence needed for attention. The second part (relation to text annotations) is answered by the Bahdanau et al. paper, which defines annotations as a sequence of vectors each focusing on a specific position in the source sentence. Solving the first part relies on the concept from the second part—without knowing that annotations must be position‑specific, one cannot justify why spatially localized vectors are necessary. Therefore the sub‑questions are not independent; the answer must synthesize information from both papers, making the question non‑decomposable and satisfying the GOOD criterion.

evidenceNeeded: A definition of "annotation vectors" as localized representations of input elements (words or image regions) that the attention mechanism can weight individually.
The requirement in sequence‑to‑sequence attention models that the encoder output a sequence of such annotations rather than a single global vector, so the decoder can attend to specific positions.
In image captioning, the encoder must produce annotation vectors that preserve spatial correspondence to parts of the image; therefore they must be taken from a lower convolutional feature map.
Why a fully‑connected layer is unsuitable for this purpose (it collapses the spatial layout into one global vector, destroying the one‑to‑one mapping needed for attention).
How the structural requirement for image annotations mirrors the textual case: each annotation corresponds to a distinct position (word or image patch) that can be selectively attended to.

The Show, Attend and Tell paper explicitly states that the encoder extracts annotation vectors from a lower convolutional layer (the 4th conv layer before max‑pooling) so that each vector corresponds to a specific part of the 2‑D image and the decoder can selectively focus on a subset of these vectors ("This allows the decoder to selectively focus on certain parts of an image by selecting a subset of all the feature vectors"). It also contrasts this with using a fully‑connected layer, which would lose the spatial correspondence needed for attention. 

The Neural Machine Translation paper defines the notion of "annotations" in sequence‑to‑sequence attention: the encoder maps the source sentence to a sequence of annotation vectors, each containing information about the whole input but with a strong focus on the surrounding words of a particular position ("Each annotation contains information about the whole input sequence with a strong focus on the parts surrounding the i‑th word"). The decoder computes a context vector as a weighted sum of these annotations ("The context vector ... is then computed as a weighted sum of these annotations"). 

By providing annotation vectors from a lower convolutional feature map, the image encoder creates a set of spatially localized vectors analogous to the per‑word annotation vectors in text. This structural similarity satisfies the same requirement of the attention mechanism: a collection of position‑specific representations over which the decoder can compute attention weights and form a context vector. Therefore the need for lower‑layer convolutional features directly mirrors the properties of textual annotations in seq2seq attention models.

2.contextPassage: In a captioning model, attention plays the role of connecting the image encoder and language decoder. The attention module normally takes the image feature map and context as input, and outputs a feature vector. In , an MLP is applied to learn the correspondence between words and image areas. When generating the current word, the attention module first computes an image representation by using the previous hidden state of the LSTM, and then the image representation and current hidden state are used to make predictions.

2.contextPassage: : The goal of the image encoder is to obtain a feature representation of an image. In this paper, we adopt an Image-CNN to extract visual features, which is similar to other image captioning models , , ,. The main difference is that our GHA is able to use convolutional feature maps at different levels, which is shown in Figure REF. Different convolutional feature maps have different receptive fields, and a feature map at lower layer can “see” smaller objects and more details of an image, while high-layer feature maps “see” parts of large objects or even the entire object.

2.contextPassage: The main difference is that our GHA is able to use convolutional feature maps at different levels, which is shown in Figure REF. Different convolutional feature maps have different receptive fields, and a feature map at lower layer can “see” smaller objects and more details of an image, while high-layer feature maps “see” parts of large objects or even the entire object. Therefore, applying multiple feature maps is able to benefit object recognition and word prediction. The image feature maps at different levels are projected to the same channel-dimension using a learnable linear transformation. Thus, an image is represented by a set of feature maps {{formula:a2f6657b-865a-4e94-9e28-c2050c9d1560}} , where {{formula:7a3f31b1-0061-44fe-aa76-e1283b35fc5f}} is the image feature vector at image position {{formula:585bc080-7adc-40dc-bc70-3e822a0e7747}} for layer {{formula:b4846f8c-0ccd-4085-88c6-0f870aa79ba4}}.

2.contextPassage: Image Captioning with Attention Mechanisms: Much work has shown that attention is able to significantly improve the captioning results , ,. In a captioning model, attention plays the role of connecting the image encoder and language decoder. The attention module normally takes the image feature map and context as input, and outputs a feature vector. In , an MLP is applied to learn the correspondence between words and image areas. When generating the current word, the attention module first computes an image representation by using the previous hidden state of the LSTM, and then the image representation and current hidden state are used to make predictions.

2.contextPassage: The goal of the image encoder is to obtain a feature representation of an image. In this paper, we adopt an Image-CNN to extract visual features, which is similar to other image captioning models , , , . The main difference is that our GHA is able to use convolutional feature maps at different levels, which is shown in Figure REF . Different convolutional feature maps have different receptive fields, and a feature map at lower layer can “see” smaller objects and more details of an image, while high-layer feature maps “see” parts of large objects or even the entire object. Therefore, applying multiple feature maps is able to benefit object recognition and word prediction .

1.contextPassage: We use a convolutional neural network in order to extract a set of feature vectors which we refer to as annotation vectors. The extractor produces {{formula:77d7a5d7-ad66-4222-88e2-013e9b7810b8}} vectors, each of which is a D-dimensional representation corresponding to a part of the image. {{formula:76c96bb5-c91a-42cf-bf94-6a661952447a}}In order to obtain a correspondence between the feature vectors and portions of the 2-D image, we extract features from a lower convolutional layer unlike previous work which instead used a fully connected layer. This allows the decoder to selectively focus on certain parts of an image by selecting a subset of all the feature vectors.

This is especially important when there is a lot of clutter in an image. Using representations (such as those from the top layer of a convnet) that distill information in image down to the most salient objects is one effective solution that has been widely adopted in previous work.

2.contextPassage: Intuitively, this implements a mechanism of attention in the decoder. The decoder decides parts of the source sentence to pay attention to. By letting the decoder have an attention mechanism, we relieve the encoder from the burden of having to encode all information in the source sentence into a fixed-length vector. With this new approach the information can be spread throughout the sequence of annotations, which can be selectively retrieved by the decoder accordingly.

1.contextPassage: We use a convolutional neural network in order to extract a set of feature vectors which we refer to as annotation vectors. The extractor produces {{formula:77d7a5d7-ad66-4222-88e2-013e9b7810b8}} vectors, each of which is a D-dimensional representation corresponding to a part of the image. {{formula:76c96bb5-c91a-42cf-bf94-6a661952447a}}In order to obtain a correspondence between the feature vectors and portions of the 2-D image, we extract features from a lower convolutional layer unlike previous work which instead used a fully connected layer. This allows the decoder to selectively focus on certain parts of an image by selecting a subset of all the feature vectors.

2.contextPassage: Intuitively, this implements a mechanism of attention in the decoder. The decoder decides parts of the source sentence to pay attention to. By letting the decoder have an attention mechanism, we relieve the encoder from the burden of having to encode all information in the source sentence into a fixed-length vector. With this new approach the information can be spread throughout the sequence of annotations, which can be selectively retrieved by the decoder accordingly.

Title: Gated Hierarchical Attention for Image Captioning

[TOP 21322 chars]: Gated Hierarchical Attention for Image Captioning
abstract: Attention modules connecting encoder and decoders have been widely applied in the field of object recognition, image captioning, visual question answering and neural machine translation, and significantly improves the performance. In this paper, we propose a bottom-up gated hierarchical attention (GHA) mechanism for image captioning. Our proposed model employs a CNN as the decoder which is able to learn different concepts at different layers, and apparently, different concepts correspond to different areas of an image. Therefore, we develop the GHA in which low-level concepts are merged into high-level concepts and simultaneously low-level attended features pass to the top to make predictions. Our GHA significantly improves the performance of the model that only applies one level attention, for example, the CIDEr score increases from 0.923 to 0.999, which is comparable to the state-of-the-art models that employ attributes boosting and reinforcement learning (RL). We also conduct extensive experiments to analyze the CNN decoder and our proposed GHA, and we find that deeper decoders cannot obtain better performance, and when the convolutional decoder becomes deeper the model is likely to collapse during training.
Introduction: Image captioning aims to automatically generate sentences that are able to describe images. To achieve this goal, an image captioning model should contain at least three parts: 1) a vision module, which extracts features from images, 2) a language module, which is used to model the sentences, 3) a connection module, which is applied to fuse the vision and language context information.Recently, CNNs are the most popular vision module, such as VGG nets , Google nets and residual nets (in this paper, we call them Image-CNNs). It is believed that introducing more information benefits the performance, and hence some models employ object detection or transfer image features into attributes to obtain more details or semantic information of an image , , , , , . However, applying object detection or attributes boosting methods requires more annotations, such as the bounding boxes of the objects and their attributes, categories and actions, which is difficult to obtain. For the language module, LSTMs dominate the field of sentence generation , , , . Almost all previous image captioning models employ LSTMs or their variants. LSTMs apply gates and a memory cell to fuse the information of a sequence of words. In contrast, treating the sequence of word embeddings as a matrix, CNNs stack multiple convolution layers to merge words together into higher-level concepts (in this paper, we call these Word-CNNs). While it is difficult to implement LSTMs in a parallel way, because there is a recurrent path during the computation, Word-CNNs only stack several layers and each layer is computed in parallel, increasing the speed. For example, to obtain the representation of 12 words, an LSTM needs 12 steps, while a Word-CNN with kernel size 3 only needs 6 layers. In terms of the connection module, a naive approach is to directly concatenate the image features and language context . However different words correspond to different areas of an image, which limits the accuracy of the naive approach. The NIC model first transfers the image features into another space at the first LSTM step and it outperforms m-RNN model . However, , are not able to learn the correspondence between words and image areas. To address this issue, introduces an attention mechanism to the LSTM-based captioning models, which is able to learn the relationship between words and image areas, and the performance improves.The connection module plays a crucial role in image captioning models and the attention mechanism leads to both better performance and also better interpretation. For example, when a captioning model generates the word “person”, the model will pay more attention to the area of the person – moreover it can also learn to find the appropriate image areas corresponding to the words that do not refer to objects. Word-CNNs are able to merge words to form high-level concepts, which mimics the tree structure of the sentence. Here we assume that each concept should correspond to an area of an image (e.g., as noted by image-text retrieval models , ), and that multi-level attention is able to provide more accurate and detailed information , , , .Inspired by , , we propose a gated hierarchical attention mechanism (GHA) for image captioning. The difference between our proposed GHA and other popular attention mechanisms is that GHA allows multi-level interaction between image encoder and language decoder, and the gating mechanism is applied to select low-level attention features and pass them to the high-level ones. Applying the proposed GHA, we obtain an increase of CIDEr score by 8.2% and SPICE by 8.6% on MSCOCO dataset, and obtain comparable results to the state-of-the-art models. Another contribution of this paper is that we conduct extensive experiments to analyze the proposed GHA and Word-CNNs.
Image Captioning with Attention Mechanisms: Much work has shown that attention is able to significantly improve the captioning results , , . In a captioning model, attention plays the role of connecting the image encoder and language decoder. The attention module normally takes the image feature map and context as input, and outputs a feature vector. In , an MLP is applied to learn the correspondence between words and image areas. When generating the current word, the attention module first computes an image representation by using the previous hidden state of the LSTM, and then the image representation and current hidden state are used to make predictions. After training, the attention module is able to show interpretable results. However, this attention mechanism computes attention feature for each word which is unreasonable because some words in the captions do not correspond to any object in an image. For example, the words “a” and “of” do not refer to any object, and therefore they are more likely to depend on the context instead of the image. To solve this problem, introduces a visual sentinel to the attention module, which is a gate that decides whether the context or the attention feature is used to predict the current word. Other attention variants apply semantic, attribute and object detection results to introduce more information , , . Generally, using more information results in better performance. In , multiple convolutional maps are employed to improve video captioning, which is similar to our GHA model. The decoder in is an LSTM and to compute the attention maps at each time step, the same LSTM hidden state is applied. In contrast, our GHA model employs convolutional decoders, and therefore different concept representations are applied to compute attention maps, which reveals more about the relationships between concepts and image regions.Moreover, our GHA model is able to obtain more visual information and hierarchically pass it from the bottom to the top level, while other models only employ attention at one layer. Although some models use gates, such as , the goals are different. The gates in our GHA filter out low-level information that cannot benefit prediction of the current word. In contrast, in , the gates decide whether the current word should depend on the image feature or the previous words. Moreover, in , all channels share the same gate, whereas, in our proposed GHA, a separate gate is used for each channel.
Word-CNNs for NLP: Word-CNNs have been widely applied in the field of NLP (e.g., text classification , , language modeling , and machine translation ) due to several advantages: 1) convolution is faster than LSTMs, because convolution can be easily computed in parallel; 2) CNNs imitate a tree structure of the sentence, which is able to benefit solving NLP tasks.In , a language CNN is applied to improve the long-term memory of LSTMs, however it also employs an LSTM to generate captions. , drop LSTMs and only apply CNNs to generate captions, which shows faster training. Although , both compute attention features at each convolutional layer, they use simple attention mechanisms, which just concatenates or adds low-level attended visual features to the high-level concept features. One disadvantage of this simple approach is that when the model becomes deeper, the influence of low-level features could vanish. Another disadvantage is that sometimes the predictions only depend on high-level features, and introducing low-level features could result in unexpected predictions. In contrast, our GHA employs a gated recurrent unit (GRU) to learn to memorize or forget low-level features. Our proposed GHA first fuses the low-level concept features and the corresponding visual attention features, and then uses joint representations to calculate gates which decide which low-level concept and visual feature can pass to higher levels. By applying the fuse-select procedure, our proposed model with GHA outperforms other image captioning models that employ CNNs. {{figure:88c905fa-6a27-4a72-aca1-0eeb3d6c75e0}}
Gated Hierarchical Attention: In this section, we present our captioning model with gated-hierarchical attention (GHA). There are four parts in our proposed GHA model: 1) image encoder, 2) visual attention, 3) causal convolutional decoder, and 4) fusing block. An overview of the proposed GHA model is shown in Figure REF . The image encoder and word decoder drive the visual attention to extract relevant features from the image feature maps. At each level, the fusing block plays the role of information fusion and selection, which allows interactions between Image-CNNs and Word-CNNs. There are gates between layer {{formula:7c604aee-f033-40a7-8233-6f01bcbd77cb}} and layer {{formula:1cacf6ac-15a9-449e-ac18-d1efb8ab86e3}} , which controls the bottom-up flow of visual and language information. The gates depend on both low-level visual and language features, and more details are in the following sections.
Image encoder.: The goal of the image encoder is to obtain a feature representation of an image. In this paper, we adopt an Image-CNN to extract visual features, which is similar to other image captioning models , , , . The main difference is that our GHA is able to use convolutional feature maps at different levels, which is shown in Figure REF . Different convolutional feature maps have different receptive fields, and a feature map at lower layer can “see” smaller objects and more details of an image, while high-layer feature maps “see” parts of large objects or even the entire object. Therefore, applying multiple feature maps is able to benefit object recognition and word prediction . The image feature maps at different levels are projected to the same channel-dimension using a learnable linear transformation. Thus, an image is represented by a set of feature maps {{formula:a2f6657b-865a-4e94-9e28-c2050c9d1560}} , where {{formula:7a3f31b1-0061-44fe-aa76-e1283b35fc5f}} is the image feature vector at image position {{formula:585bc080-7adc-40dc-bc70-3e822a0e7747}} for layer {{formula:b4846f8c-0ccd-4085-88c6-0f870aa79ba4}} .
Causal Word-CNNs.: The goal of Word-CNNs is to merge words to obtain a high-level representation of the sentence. Since we do not know the future words during inference time, we employ causal convolution, which only considers the previous words. In this paper, the Word-CNNs stack multiple causal convolutional layers (see Figure REF , which shows a decoder with kernel size 3). The Word-CNN produces a set of concept representations at different levels, {{formula:c84456b9-cf83-4edc-8172-8bad8441f842}} , where {{formula:0698745d-2685-4b95-8cf5-404961da8db3}} is the concept vector for level {{formula:e98ffb9f-893f-4cd9-a3eb-316c40164cf6}} and position {{formula:247003ab-0161-4c02-82c6-98aad7c0d180}} . {{formula:c9ff0aa2-3a02-43f8-af2c-e34ec635d30c}} is the number of the convolutional layers in our decoder CNN, and {{formula:af282311-28d9-4b1f-a063-ddb231b2c0e7}} is the word embedding layer. {{formula:5da9901f-0d1b-4422-9e20-240e4f7a7b68}} is the length of a caption.For the activation function, gated linear units (GLU) show more advantages than ReLU in NLP , and other convolutional image captioning models also employ GLU , . In a standard GLU, both the gates and linear activations are computed using the hidden states of the previous layer of the decoder. For our GHA, we use a variant of GLU where the previous decoder layer is used to drive the linear unit and the fusing block is used to drive the gate, {{formula:5f0269bb-120d-4043-90a5-baeea29d6865}}where {{formula:84a425e1-060e-4abf-9ac0-9baf337980a3}} is the concepts at the {{formula:7d723b2e-844f-4a3a-986a-f6610eb96236}} -th layer of the decoder, and {{formula:97713f70-e155-4d0b-a7bf-202080106693}} is the hidden state of the fusing block (described later). {{formula:725ab8eb-ed5e-44de-80ac-507012f758b5}} denotes convolution, {{formula:cbe0241b-5393-48d0-920c-11b0c0059267}} is element-wise multiplication, and {{formula:6a9bd3b7-a40f-4cac-8e1e-788a9070724d}} are trainable weights. The advantage of using {{formula:dd8880d2-2c59-4d6b-ab15-eee6a665ba4f}} instead of {{formula:7f72b824-298b-48b6-bd59-32f4b1f7b565}} for the gate is that the visual attention feature {{formula:d5ced14a-26b3-407b-931f-9765c8c41990}} are able to decide which concept features can pass to higher levels, resulting in more significant interaction between concepts and visual features.
Visual attention.: The visual attention module aims to learn the correspondence between concepts and image areas. In our GHA, the visual attention feature {{formula:23bf7c24-1420-444e-b115-342c4dcd355e}} at {{formula:1225551a-f2e1-46ab-9177-9eaa2c1526c4}} -th level is composed of two partsFor the word embedding layer {{formula:52c8d21b-b79e-4c6a-be57-bff755d660b3}} , only the first part is used.: 1) the current level visual attention feature {{formula:a77d3190-19e7-4714-91ed-3149b80732dd}} , 2) the previous level attention feature {{formula:d46aa457-f710-45f1-a209-3ed3169ac579}} . The current-level attention feature {{formula:680880a2-9293-4e08-a90c-9457d18400eb}} is calculated using the concepts {{formula:4259e417-0d90-4e53-913a-ab36753fcb0b}} at the same level: {{formula:010671e8-3431-4b18-9f17-ca399435c048}}where {{formula:05a01062-f9d4-42fc-baf2-56e02b2d7360}} is a parameter matrix. Note that, similar to , we apply a scaling factor {{formula:b47c526d-6447-4aec-8540-342e22515377}} to {{formula:184ddcd1-06a7-4dca-9732-2794168c898b}} since it might take large values.The final visual attention feature {{formula:41190bdc-52e6-4864-9cdf-ce5f60414768}} is computed as follows: {{formula:a84ec56f-d08b-496c-b964-df09963edf81}}where {{formula:42008ec0-b76b-450a-8144-10243d934694}} is the hidden state of the fusing block, and {{formula:0858211b-27be-4f6e-9a97-45cdf025b56e}} are the trainable parameters. By using gates, GHA is able to select lower-level visual attention features ({{formula:0539f48f-4132-4aa6-aecc-8cb9e1eee433}} ) and fuse them with current (higher) level features ({{formula:5aeb80d2-74f7-44ff-aa17-c0a69cd5b71b}} ).
Fusing block.: The motivation of our GHA is to generate different level visual attention features for different concepts and pass low-level features to higher levels. To achieve the goal, we use a GRU to fuse the low-level concepts and the corresponding visual attention features. Concatenating the visual attention features and concepts {{formula:fa454164-ce64-4824-8c58-d68f53f31f03}} , the hidden state of the fusing block {{formula:f38f74f8-7fc9-4f38-b7bb-ac7207718245}} is computed as follows: {{formula:ee97317a-3ab1-4ee0-8d85-6d41811f60fd}}where the initial hidden state is {{formula:077c080f-1613-4013-9107-f72ec9413bdf}} . Note that we apply GRUs in a different way. Normally, GRUs are employed to modeling sequences, and thus the recurrent path is along with the time axis. In contrast, in our fusing block the recurrent path is along the hierarchical levels, from bottom to top.
Prediction and Loss Function.: We employ a 3-layer MLP to predict the next word at sentence position {{formula:95f69e01-5643-4580-9886-780874cfba48}} . Dropout layers are also applied to mitigate overfitting. At the {{formula:aa5d4783-b71b-4826-a296-de0d46d830b5}} -th position, the prediction MLP takes {{formula:a552dcd4-20e1-4a96-a0a0-6c9aa8956777}} and {{formula:3628df7e-a4a6-47ab-bbb3-104e5b798ac4}} as input, and outputs the probability distribution {{formula:aeb66850-04b5-4d93-bcb3-0da79a7edb36}} of the next word. The loss function is the cross-entropy loss between {{formula:f9632cf1-17df-464b-9722-14a55c44bbeb}} and the ground-truth words in the sentence.
Dataset and Preprocessing: In this paper, we conduct experiments on MSCOCO dataset , which contains 82,783 training and 40,504 validation images, where each image has at least 5 captions.
